Since the survival of the Qur'an and the hadith has been decreed, there is no need for a new prophet, messenger or vicegerent, and no room for a new law.

Fourth, because the vicegerency of the last Prophet ﷺ continues to the end of time, those who succeed him in preserving spiritual and temporal order are not vicegerents of Allah but vicegerents and deputies of the Prophet ﷺ. A hadith reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim says that the Israelites were governed by their prophets, and whenever a prophet died another took his place, but that no prophet will come after him, and instead there will be his deputies (khulafāʾ), and they will be many.

Fifth, Allah has ordained that after the Prophet ﷺ his Ummah as a body should enjoy a privilege that had belonged to the prophets. The community as a whole has been declared protected from error and placed under Allah's special care, so that it will never unanimously agree on a doctrinal error or deviation. A decision reached in religious matters by the consensus of the Ummah is therefore a manifestation of divine command, and consensus is accepted as the third foundation of the Sharīʿah after the Qur'an and the hadith. The Prophet ﷺ himself said that his Ummah will never collectively agree upon error. Another hadith, already mentioned, promises that however much the world changes and however indifferent people become to the truth, a group within the Ummah will always defend and preserve it and will finally prevail.

### The caliphate after the Prophet ﷺ

Since the Ummah as a body cannot go astray, the responsibility of choosing a deputy to the Prophet ﷺ has been entrusted to it. The legitimate way of governing the earth is for the Ummah to select a khalīfah who, once chosen, bears sole responsibility for maintaining spiritual and temporal order. One khalīfah for the entire world is also possible.

The first to succeed the Prophet ﷺ as his deputies were the four great caliphs known as al-Khulafāʾ ar-Rāshidīn, the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, and the order of the caliphate functioned according to its proper principles up to the end of their time. Their decisions are therefore not merely temporary judgments but carry permanent legislative value and an authority of their own degree, for the Prophet ﷺ said to hold fast to his way and to the way of the rightly-guided caliphs.

After their age, different rulers appeared in different regions, and none of them can properly be called the khalīfah of the whole Muslim community, though each may be called the amīr of his region. Once agreement by all the world's Muslims on a single man became practically impossible, and separate rulers for separate regions became customary, people accepted the principle that whoever was chosen or acknowledged by the majority of the Muslims of a country should be its amīr. The basis for this is given by the Qur'an itself in its description of the believers as those "who respond to their Lord, establish prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation, and donate from what We have provided for them" (42:38). Modern legislative assemblies are a form of mutual consultation too, but with a crucial difference. They are free to make whatever laws they please according to their own opinion, whereas an Islamic assembly, its members and their amīr are all bound by the law Allah sent through the Prophet ﷺ. There are specific conditions for membership in such an assembly and for the choice of an amīr, and above all its laws must stay within the basic principles laid down by the Qur'an and the Sunnah, whose authority the assembly has no right to question.

The whole discussion can be summarised in five principles. Sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone. The task of establishing His commandments on the earth is carried out by a vicegerent who is at the same time His messenger and prophet. The chain of such vicegerents ended with the Prophet ﷺ, the last Messenger and Prophet. The function of vicegerency is now carried out by the deputies of the Prophet ﷺ. And such a deputy, the khalīfah, is to be chosen by the Muslim community.

### Rulings on appointing a leader

Al-Qurṭubī and other scholars said that this verse proves the obligation of appointing a khalīfah to judge disputes among people, to support the oppressed against the oppressor, to apply the penal law and to forbid evil. Many other duties can be fulfilled only by appointing an imām, and whatever is necessary for performing an obligation is itself obligatory.

The leadership can come about in several ways. A group among the scholars of Ahl as-Sunnah held that the Prophet ﷺ named Abū Bakr as his successor, or at least indicated him. A sitting khalīfah may name his successor, as Abū Bakr did with ʿUmar. He may leave the choice to a consultative council of righteous men, as ʿUmar did. Or the people of authority may gather around one man and give him their pledge of allegiance, or appoint one of their number to select the candidate, which is the view of the majority.

The khalīfah must be a responsible adult Muslim male, capable of ijtihād, independent legal reasoning, physically able, upright, and knowledgeable in warfare and politics. According to the correct view he must be from Quraysh, but he need not be from Banū Hāshim, nor need he be protected from error, as the Rāfiḍah falsely claim.

Should a khalīfah who becomes immoral, a fāsiq, be removed? Scholars disagree, but the correct view is that he is not to be deposed, because of the Prophet's ﷺ words that obedience is owed unless you witness clear disbelief for which you have clear proof from Allah. May a khalīfah resign? Here too there is a difference. It is a fact that al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī gave up the position and surrendered it to Muʿāwiyah, but he did so out of necessity, and he was praised for it.

It is not permissible to appoint two or more imāms over the world at the same time, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that whoever comes to you while you are united and tries to divide you should be put to death, whoever he may be. This is the position of the majority. Imām al-Ḥaramayn related that Abū Isḥāq allowed two or more imāms when the provinces are far apart, but Imām al-Ḥaramayn himself was undecided about that view.

### Two modern misreadings

Two distortions of this verse have gained currency in modern times and need to be answered.

The first is the habit of some modernists of reading these verses as if man's vicegerency meant a duty to advance in science, meaning the empirical study of the physical world. One self-described Muslim translator of the Qur'an even went so far as to translate the name Ādam by the English word "Man," thereby denying the existence and the prophethood of Ādam. Against such errors it must be said that the names Allah taught Ādam do not refer merely to the chemical, biological or psychological properties of things and people, but to their essential qualities and aptitudes, in the technical, metaphysical sense of "essential" that the word originally had in the West as well. Mawlānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī adds in his Bayān al-Qurʾān that knowledge of the names even includes knowledge of the rulings of the Sharīʿah that distinguish the lawful from the unlawful. Many great Sufis hold that Ādam was given knowledge of the names of Allah, not all the divine names in detail, since a created being cannot comprehend the Infinite, but the divine names in summary form, and this interpretation was advanced by so reliable a scholar as Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh of Pānīpat in his Tafsīr al-Maẓharī. The subtle point behind it is that everything that exists reflects some divine attribute, which in turn manifests a divine name. The divine names are thus the essential principles and roots of all things, and whoever knows them knows things in their inner natures.

The second distortion is more serious. Under the influence of Western humanism, and in their general indifference to doctrine, modernists have come to identify the prophet Ādam, the father of mankind, entirely with the biological species "man," and to claim that every individual of the species, unconditionally and without qualification, is born a vicegerent of Allah. The error has been fed by a careless misreading of Sufi metaphysical texts and poetry. What these writers have never troubled to learn is that there are degrees, and that the degrees differ. The Sufis do often speak of "man" as Allah's vicegerent, but what they mean is no biological organism or species. They mean al-Insān al-Kāmil, the Universal Man, a term the orientalists wrongly rendered "the perfect man," importing ethical connotations into a sphere of pure metaphysics. In Sufi prose and poetry "Man" also stands for the total and essential reality of man (al-Ḥaqīqah al-Jāmiʿah al-Insāniyyah). The Universal Man par excellence is the Prophet ﷺ. This is the first degree of "manhood," and to it belong the awliyāʾ, the great friends of Allah, and those rulers who dispensed justice according to the Sharīʿah. Lower degrees follow: the pious and virtuous Muslims, and at the bottom those who are sinful but, as Muslims, may still hope for salvation. Allah alone knows who belongs to which degree, and below the degree of the Companions one can never speak with certainty. If vicegerency is attributed to an ordinary Muslim at all, it is vicegerency by reflection, just as the īmān of every Muslim is a reflection of the īmān of the Prophet ﷺ. The necessary condition for receiving even a faint reflection of vicegerency and "manhood" is that one be a Muslim, for the Qur'an declares that Allah will now accept no faith except Islam. As for attributing vicegerency to the ordinary human being as such, it can at best be vicegerency in potency, to use Aristotle's terms, not in act, and it cannot become effective without total submission to the Sharīʿah, strenuous spiritual effort and patient waiting upon the grace of Allah. In truth the highest excellence open to a human being now is to be, in word, deed and thought, a perfect follower of the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.

### A reading for the inner life

The Sufis retell this verse as a drama of love. Picture a world at rest, with no heart yet burning in passion and no breast yet deluded by wild fervour. Then the ocean of mercy started to boil. The treasuries of obedient deeds stood full, and the foreheads of the obedient carried no dust of weariness. The banner of their proud claim, "We glorify Your praise," was raised as high as the star Capella. Every subtle being in the cosmos began to crave the honour for itself. The majestic Throne looked at its own vastness and said, "Perhaps these words are written for me." The Footstool looked at its own breadth: "Perhaps this sermon is read in my name." The eight paradises gazed at their own beauty: "Maybe this rulership will be given to us." None of them wanted anything to do with dust. Each fell into its own delusion.

Suddenly, from the Presence of Exaltation and Majesty, the report reached the world of the angels: "I am going to place a vicegerent on earth." This was no consultation with the angels. Allah was laying the foundation of Ādam's exaltation and spreading the carpet of his dignity. It was as if He said: My severity has done its work. I have ordered the pen of generosity to write one inscription across the world's ledger from first page to last, binding on everyone in both worlds, from the Throne's summit down to the Carpet, and it reads: Ādam of the dust is made chief over all the kingdoms, his breast will shine with the light of recognition, and in him the subtleties of My generosity and the artefacts of My bounty will be put on display.

This declaration made the hearts of the angels nearest to Allah quake with awe. They said, "What is this about? He has not even been created yet." Before he had entered the bonds of creation, the drum of his vicegerency was already sounding at the threshold of his beauty. From the hidden affairs of the Unseen the majesty of predetermination announced: keep away from the field of Ādam's good fortune, because the secret of his innate disposition is beyond you. On the branch of that good fortune no falcon of any mind has perched, and the beauty of his clear sun no eye of insight has taken in.

Where did this eminence come from? It came from Ādam being the oyster shell that held the mysteries of lordship, the treasury that held the jewels of the kingdom. Countless precious pearls and royal gems were laid in that shell. Yet next to every pearl a black bead was strung, and every prophet's pearl was given its dark counterpart. Ādam the chosen had Satan the wretched. Ibrāhīm (Abraham) the intimate friend had Nimrod the rebel. Mūsā son of ʿImrān had Pharaoh the forsaken. ʿĪsā son of Maryam had a tribe steeped in misguidance and transgression. And the Arab Muṣṭafā ﷺ had Abū Jahl, the man full of ignorance.

This terrifying declaration drove calm and repose out of the angels, and their intellects and their patience lost all composure. They cried out together: "Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?" O Lord, they said, O King, O Magnanimous, O Creator, this Ādam of the dust will stain the embroidered robe of nearness with disobedience. He will pull his head out of the collar of obedience. You created us from holiness and the declaring of holiness, You adorned our breasts with reciting the formula of tawḥīd and with glorification, You made all of this our means!" It is said that a fire came forth from the hidden affairs of the Unseen and consumed a tribe of the angels.

Then came the declaration in the attribute of exaltedness: "I know what you do not know." You who are gazers, keep on gazing. The secret treasuries of divinity are no business of yours, and the hidden affairs of Our unseen lordship are not yours to meddle in. We alone know what Our divinity has prepared and what mysteries Our lordship conceals. Puny minds, the sciences and intellects of anyone but Us, defective understandings, insights that arrived only yesterday: how could any of these find a path to the mysteries of Our divinity? "With Him are the keys of the unseen, no one knows them except Him" (6:59). Before all beginnings We decreed that the lamp of the realities of recognition would be lit in the breast of Ādam of the dust, that the edict of rulership would pass into his hand, and that the flag of the earthly kingdoms would be planted in his soldierly heart.

And the angels were given their orders. You who are the nearest angels of the kingdom, be serving-boys, lay the carpet before the throne of his good fortune, and fall down in prostration before him. You who circle Our Throne, ask forgiveness for the sins of Ādam's progeny that have not yet been committed by people who do not yet exist, and ask safety for their going forth, saying, "Peace be upon them, peace be upon them," so that once they exist their feet will not slip on servanthood's carpet. You who keep the veils, weep for the heedless among Ādam's progeny, so that because of your weeping We may cover their disobedience with Our forgiveness. You who are the folk of the cushions, fill water-bags of light from this pure water whose waves lap around Our Throne, and when they lift their thirsty heads from the earth on the Day of Resurrection, give them to drink. You who are the sinless ones of the Lote Tree of the Furthest Boundary, wait until the Greatest Terror appears at the Resurrection, when awe and the seizing and grasping of punishment come forth, and then grant the faithful among them safety from that terror and carry to them Our greeting of peace. Every one of these commands is given so that you angels will learn the eminence of these dust-dwellers and raise no protest against Our decree.

There is a sound report that the Supreme Assembly, the angels nearest the Exalted Threshold, said, "O Lord, You have given the dust-dwellers the low world. Give us the high world, for we are the birds of the Presence and the peacocks of the Exalted Threshold." The answer came: the wholesome progeny of the one whom My own two hands created will never be made like those who came to be when I merely said "Be!" I am the intimate of passion, and you are merely passing by, unaware of the tale and the state of the passionate. Why do you grieve over the ugliness of My beloved? Come into My eyes and look at him.

### In short

- Allah announced to the angels, before creating Ādam, that He would place a khalīfah on the earth: a successor to those before, a deputy who applies His rulings, and the father of generations that replace one another (6:165, 27:62, 43:60).
- The angels asked, not in objection but to learn the wisdom, why a creature capable of corruption and bloodshed should be preferred to beings who glorify and sanctify Allah without pause. Allah answered that He knows what they do not: among Ādam's children would be prophets, martyrs, the righteous and lovers of Allah, and the capacity for evil is exactly why a restraining deputy is needed.
- The announcement in the form of a consultation teaches the value of mutual consultation and exposed the angels' assumption that nothing more knowledgeable than they would ever be created.
- From the verse scholars derive the principles of governance: sovereignty is Allah's alone, vicegerents are chosen by Him, the chain ended with the Prophet ﷺ, and after him the Ummah chooses his deputies, with the obligation, methods and conditions of the caliphate spelled out by the jurists.
- Vicegerency belongs to the Prophet ﷺ, the awliyāʾ and just rulers in the fullest sense, and to the ordinary Muslim only by reflection. It is not a licence for every human being as such, nor a charter for scientific progress.

31.text:
Allah had told the angels, "I know what you do not know." This verse begins the demonstration that proved it. "He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, 'Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?'" The angels had assumed that no creature could outrank them in knowledge, and that beings who glorify and sanctify Allah without pause were better suited to be His vicegerents than a creature who would shed blood. Instead of simply overruling them, Allah set a test that showed them, in a way they could not dispute, that Ādam (Adam) possessed a kind of knowledge they lacked. The verse therefore states the virtue of Ādam over the angels: Allah taught him, and not them, the names of everything. One view holds that this teaching actually took place after the angels prostrated to him, and that it is mentioned first only to underline the importance of his rank and to show how little the angels knew about the vicegerent when they asked about him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He taught Adam the names of all things"** is explained in several ways, which build on one another. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said it means the words people use for things: human, animal, sky, earth, land, sea, horse, donkey, and so on through every other kind of creature. Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr reported through ʿĀṣim ibn Kulayb, from Saʿīd ibn Maʿbad, that Ibn ʿAbbās was asked whether Allah taught Ādam the names of the plate and the pot, and he answered, "Yes, and even the words for breaking wind." So Allah taught Ādam the proper names of everything, the names of their qualities, and the words for what they do, down to the homeliest words in the language. Others say the names were those of all his descendants, or of all the animals and other things including a cooking pot, a plate and a saucer. Taken together, the teaching covered living things and objects, their pronunciation and their meanings, and the knowledge was placed directly into his heart. The Arabic is doubly emphatic: "names" is a general term that already implies comprehensiveness, and "all of them" adds that nothing was left out and that each meaning was fully verified.

A hadith confirms that the teaching embraced the names of all creatures. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, in the Book of Tafsīr, al-Bukhārī explained this verse with a report from Anas ibn Mālik that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the great intercession on the Day of Resurrection. The believers will gather and agree to seek someone to intercede for them with their Lord. They will come to Ādam and say: you are the father of the whole human race, Allah created you with His own Hand, had the angels prostrate to you and taught you the names of everything, so will you not intercede for us so that we are relieved of this standing place? Ādam will remember his error, feel ashamed, and tell them he is not the one for this. He will send them to Nūḥ (Noah), the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth. Nūḥ will recall having asked Allah about what he had no knowledge of, feel ashamed, and send them to Khalīl ar-Raḥmān, the intimate friend of the Most Merciful, Ibrāhīm (Abraham). Ibrāhīm will send them to Mūsā (Moses), the servant whom Allah addressed directly and to whom He gave the Tawrāh. Mūsā will remember having killed a man without right and will send them to ʿĪsā (Jesus), Allah's servant and messenger, His Word and a spirit from Him. ʿĪsā will send them to Muḥammad ﷺ, a servant whose earlier and later errors have been forgiven. The Prophet ﷺ said that he will then go to Allah, ask His permission, fall in prostration when he sees his Lord, and remain so as long as Allah wills, until he is told: Muḥammad, raise your head, ask and you will be given, intercede and your intercession will be accepted. He will praise Allah with praise that Allah inspires in him, intercede, and be granted a number of people to admit to Paradise, and he will return and do the same a second, a third and a fourth time, until he says that no one remains in Hell except those whom the Qur'an has confined there for eternity. Muslim, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah also recorded this hadith. The part that matters here is the believers' words to Ādam, "Allah taught you the names of everything," which show that the names were the names of all created things.

**"then He presented them to the angels"** means that He displayed the objects themselves, the things that had been named, before the angels. ʿAbdur-Razzāq narrated from Maʿmar that Qatādah said that Allah paraded the objects in front of them. Most of the things named were intelligent beings, which is why the Arabic uses the pronoun for rational beings. On the reading that the names were those of Ādam's descendants, the scene is this: Allah brought the whole progeny of Ādam before their first father and said to the angels, in effect, "These are the children of Ādam. Can you name each of them and say what sort of people they will be?" The word "then" (thumma) marks a pause or interval between the teaching and the presentation.

**"and said, 'Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?'"** was said in reproach. The point was to prove the angels wrong, and the question is directed at the very angels who had asked, "Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?" It is as if Allah said: you asked whether the vicegerent would be from among you or from some other creation, and you pointed to your praise and glorification. If you speak the truth in claiming that a non-angel vicegerent and his offspring will disobey Me, cause corruption and shed blood, while you, if I made you the vicegerents, would obey Me, carry out My commands and glorify Me, then tell Me the names of what I have set before you. But since you do not know even the names of these objects that are present before you, you have still less knowledge of what will happen on an earth that does not yet exist. "If what you say is true" refers to their first claim, their belief that Allah would not create anything more knowledgeable than they were, or that they were more deserving of the vicegerency, or that they were a nobler and better creation than Ādam. The answer to the conditional "if" is understood from what precedes it.

### Who gave language to human beings?

Imām al-Ashʿarī drew a conclusion from this episode: language as such was created by Allah Himself and not invented by man, and its use by different peoples later produced the many forms of language. The first speaker learned his words from his Maker.

### The names of created things and the names of the Real

Some scholars find a second layer in the verse. Just as Allah taught Ādam the names of created things, all of them, as Ibn ʿAbbās and others explain, He also taught him the names of the Real, that is, knowledge of Allah's own names and attributes. To the angels, however, He disclosed only the place He had chosen for knowledge of the names of created things, and through that disclosure the measure of Ādam's superiority over them. Ādam's uniqueness in knowing the names of Allah was a secret of which no angel, however near to Allah, was aware. If a being does not even match Ādam in knowing the names of created things, what hope has it of drawing near to the names of the Real or of grasping the unseen's secrets? And if being chosen to know the names of created things made it fitting for the angels to prostrate before him, what must be thought of being chosen to know the names of the Real, and what is owed to the one honoured with that?

On this view the special excellence of the angels lies in glorification and sanctification. Those are acts of obedience, and obedience befits created beings, since it is the mark of servants and of servants alone. Knowledge, by contrast, is a form of praise that is necessarily true of the Real and belongs properly to no one else, and among created beings none honours Allah more perfectly than the one who honours Him through Allah's own explanation of His attributes. It is also said that Allah first honoured Ādam privately with what He taught him, and then made His choice of him and his precedence public on the day he was presented to the angels.

### What the angels learned about human beings

If the things presented were the descendants of Ādam, then the demonstration also answered the angels' worry about corruption and bloodshed. When Ādam, taught by Allah, explained to the angels the names and characters of the human race, they realised that besides the wicked and the corrupt there would be great, righteous and pious souls among them. The mixture of good and evil in humanity, which had alarmed them, turned out to include the very people for whose sake the whole enterprise was worthwhile.

### In short

- To prove that He knew what the angels did not, Allah taught Ādam the names of all things, from the greatest creatures to the plate, the pot and the coarsest everyday words, then set the things before the angels and challenged them to name them.
- The challenge answered the angels' assumption that no being could surpass them in knowledge or deserve the vicegerency more than they did.
- The great intercession hadith (al-Bukhārī, Muslim, an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah) confirms that Ādam was taught the names of everything.
- Imām al-Ashʿarī concluded that language itself is Allah's creation, and the Sufis add that Ādam was also given knowledge of the names of the Real.

32.text:
Confronted with things they could not name, the angels did not argue. "They replied, 'Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.'" The verse records how perfectly obedient creatures respond when their understanding is shown to be limited: with praise first, then an admission, then an affirmation of Allah's knowledge and wisdom.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Glory be to You!"** declares Allah's holiness and His perfection above every deficiency. In context it carries several meanings at once. The angels exalt Allah above any objection anyone might raise to Him. They repent of what they had said earlier. And they acknowledge that His judgment and His sacred law cannot be doubted. They offered this praise before they made their apology, and by it they affirmed the rightness of His decree over any objection of their own. Their words also clear Allah of any suggestion that He had wronged them by asking the incapable to do what He knew they could not do, for the question had been put in order to teach, not to blame.

**"We have no knowledge except what You have taught us"** is the admission. No creature acquires any share of Allah's knowledge except by His permission, and none knows anything except what He teaches or inspires. The angels recognised their shortcoming and recognised that everything comes from Allah. They were saying: we have no knowledge of what You have asked us about, and You taught Ādam what You did not teach us.

**"You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise"** ends the reply with two names. The Arabic innaka anta is emphatic, "You, You alone." Allah knows everything about the angels and about the things presented, and nothing escapes His knowledge. He is Wise in His decrees and laws, in the angels' affairs and in the affairs of human beings, and He makes the wisest decisions, granting knowledge to whom He wills and withholding it from whom He wills. Whatever He does is true and right, no one can pass judgment over Him, and nothing foolish or ugly comes from Him. His wisdom and justice in every matter are perfect.

### What the angels' reply shows

The angels' earlier question, as the previous verses explained, was a humble inquiry and an offer of service, not a protest. Their reply here proves it. The moment another being was shown to be more suitable for the task by his special kind of knowledge, they acknowledged the fact just as humbly and withdrew their opinion. The phrase "Glory be to You" also implies that Allah is free of any charge of having withheld from the angels the knowledge He gave to Ādam, because, being All-Knowing and All-Wise, He gives each creature the kind and degree of knowledge and understanding that suits its particular nature, and He alone knows what that is.

### In short

- The angels answered their failure to name the things with praise, repentance and an admission that their knowledge is only what Allah has taught them.
- Their reply affirms that Allah's judgment and law are beyond objection and that His knowledge and wisdom are perfect.
- It models the right response to being corrected: no argument, no resentment, only glorification and surrender.

33.text:
The test now reaches its conclusion. "Allah said, 'O Adam! Inform them of their names.' Then when Adam did, Allah said, 'Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?'" Ādam (Adam) does what the angels could not, his superiority in knowledge becomes plain, and Allah reminds the angels of His earlier answer, "I know what you do not know," adding that He knows not only the unseen in the heavens and the earth but also what the angels had said aloud and what they had kept to themselves.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah said, 'O Adam! Inform them of their names'"** turns the demonstration over to Ādam. Zayd ibn Aslam said that Ādam told the angels, "You are Jibrīl, you are Mīkāʾīl, you are Isrāfīl," and so on, until he came to the name of the crow. Mujāhid said he gave the name of the pigeon, the crow and everything else, and similar explanations are reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah. He named each thing by its proper name and also mentioned the wisdom behind its creation. On the reading that the things presented were his descendants, he passed on to the angels what Allah had taught him about the nature of the human race.

There is a subtle point in the choice of words. When Allah asked the angels, He said, "Tell Me." When He commanded Ādam, He said, "Tell them." The difference shows that Ādam stood as a teacher while the angels sat as pupils, which is itself a sign of his superiority. The episode also shows that the knowledge of the angels can increase or decrease, for through Ādam they received at least an elementary knowledge of something they had not known before. Another trace of Allah's kindness to Ādam appears here. When Allah said to the angels, "Tell Me," they were seized with fear of speaking, especially because they were being asked about something their kind of knowledge did not reach. Ādam, because of what he knew, was directed to address the angels, and he was not overcome by fear in speaking to them.

**"Then when Adam did, Allah said, 'Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth'"** is spoken in rebuke once Ādam's merit had become evident. It means: did I not say that I know the seen and the unseen alike, everything hidden in the heavens and on the earth, and everything that will take place in them? It also means that Allah knows the different kinds of knowledge of created beings, which the angels do not. Allah says elsewhere, "Whether you speak openly or not, He certainly knows what is secret and what is even more hidden" (20:7), and He reports the words of the hoopoe to Sulaymān (Solomon) about those who do not prostrate to Allah, "Who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you all conceal and what you reveal. He is Allah! There is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne" (27:25-26).

**"and I know what you reveal and what you conceal"** has been explained in several ways. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said it means: I know secrets just as I know what is apparent, such as the arrogance and pride that Iblīs concealed in his heart. Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī narrated that ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said that what the angels revealed was their question, "Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?" while what they concealed was the thought, "We have more knowledge and honour than any creation our Lord will create," and they then learned that Allah had favoured Ādam over them in both knowledge and honour. Others say that what they revealed was the obedience they showed their Lord in bowing to Ādam and what they hid was the inward side of that obedience, or that the verse refers to what Satan disclosed and what he kept hidden from them. One further reading is that Allah knows the acts of obedience the angels displayed and the belief in their own superiority over Ādam that they kept hidden.

### Allah's care and Allah's decree

The whole episode shows Allah's solicitude for Ādam. When the Real wished to choose him, He guarded him, instructed him, and let him see the effects of His care, until Ādam could say what he said about the names. Yet when Allah wished to carry out His decree concerning him, He let forgetfulness enter him, so that he forgot the covenant made in Allah's presence and overstepped His limit: "And indeed, We once made a covenant with Adam, but he forgot, and so We did not find determination in him" (20:115). The moment favoured by divine care brought knowledge and goodness to their fullness, while the moment when the decree took effect returned him to forgetfulness and disobedience. Such are the decrees of the Real in what they bring and what they take away. The servant is humbled by His decree, and He is the "Doer of whatever He wills" (85:16), for "surely your Lord does what He intends" (11:107).

The angels had imagined that their glorification and sanctification would win them preference. Allah let them know that the carpet of His majesty is too holy to be adorned by the obedience of the obedient or stained by the errors of stubborn deniers. Their return to prostration before Ādam made plain that Allah has no need of the agreement or the opposition of any creature.

### Corruption and bloodshed

Since the angels' question about corruption and bloodshed hangs over these verses, one lesson about human conduct follows. After denial of one's Lord, humanity's greatest crimes are spreading corruption and shedding blood. No individual and no group has God's permission to do anything that disrupts the order of nature He established, and no one may take another's life. Actions of this kind disqualify people from God's mercy. To preserve the system of nature is to reform the earth, and to upset it is what the Qur'an calls spreading corruption.

### In short

- Ādam named everything the angels could not, from Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl and Isrāfīl down to the crow and the pigeon, and so his superiority in knowledge was proved.
- "Tell Me" to the angels and "tell them" to Ādam made Ādam the teacher and the angels the pupils.
- Allah reminded the angels that He knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth and also what they had said and what they had silently thought, including the pride hidden in Iblīs.
- Ādam's knowledge came from Allah's care, and his later lapse came from Allah's decree (20:115). Both show that Allah needs neither the agreement nor the opposition of His creatures.

34.text:
The angels had learned that Ādam (Adam) surpassed them in the knowledge needed for vicegerency on the earth. Now Allah made that superiority visible. "And remember when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate before Adam,' so they all did, but not Iblīs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful." The verse records a great honour granted to Ādam, an honour that Allah reminds his descendants of, and at the same time it records the first sin ever committed: the refusal of Iblīs, rooted in pride. Both the honour and the refusal set the pattern for everything that follows in the story of humanity.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And remember when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate before Adam'"** describes the honour. Having shown the angels that Ādam possessed what they lacked, Allah commanded them to prostrate before him as a mark of his rank, out of recognition and respect, and they obeyed eagerly. Many hadiths testify to this command, including the hadith of the intercession, in which the believers remind Ādam that Allah created him with His own Hand, made the angels prostrate to him and taught him the names of everything. There is also the hadith of the prayer of Mūsā (Moses), who asked his Lord to show him Ādam, the one who had caused himself and his descendants to leave Paradise, and who said to him when they met, "Are you Ādam, whom Allah created with His own Hands, breathed life into, and commanded the angels to prostrate before?"

Qatādah drew the essential distinction: the obedience was to Allah, and the prostration was before Ādam. Allah honoured Ādam and commanded the angels to bow to him, so the angels in bowing were worshipping Allah, not Ādam. Many scholars describe the prostration as a bow of salutation, greeting and honour rather than an act of worship, and compare it to the verse in which the parents and brothers of Yūsuf (Joseph), arriving in Egypt, "all fell down in prostration to Joseph" (12:100).

**"so they all did"** means that every angel complied. The wording of the Qur'an addresses the command to the angels alone, but by excepting Iblīs from those who obeyed, the text implies that the command was given to every being with understanding that existed at the time, the jinn included. The angels are named because when superior beings like the angels were required to show respect for Ādam, it goes without saying that lesser creatures like the jinn were required to do the same.

**"but not Iblīs"** raises the question of who Iblīs was. He was not an angel. The Qur'an says elsewhere that he "was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord" (18:50), and calls him the father of the jinn. He was included in the command given to the angels because he was living among them and imitating their conduct and their deeds, and so he was blamed for defying a command that covered him. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said that Iblīs, before he turned to sin, lived among the angels under the name ʿAzāzīl. He was one of the inhabitants of the earth, among the most devoted worshippers and most knowledgeable of those who stood with the angels, and this very distinction made him arrogant. His origin was the species called jinn. Because of the excellence of his worship, Allah had admitted him to the company of the angels, but when the test came he returned to his lowly nature. His name is explained as meaning one who was far from the truth and far from the mercy of God.

**"who refused and acted arrogantly"** gives the two faces of his sin: an outward refusal and an inward pride. He would not follow his Lord's command, and he disdained to bow, saying that he was better than Ādam because he had been created from fire and Ādam from clay. Qatādah said that Iblīs, the enemy of Allah, envied Ādam the honour Allah had given him, and that arrogance was therefore the very first sin, since pride is what kept the enemy of Allah from prostrating before Ādam. The Ṣaḥīḥ records the Prophet's ﷺ warning that no one with a mustard seed's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise. Disbelief, arrogance and rebellion together drove Iblīs out of Allah's holy presence and out of His mercy.

**"becoming unfaithful"** states the verdict. One view is that he became a disbeliever by this very act, because he refused to comply with Allah's command. Another is that in Allah's foreknowledge he had always been destined to be a disbeliever, and the verse describes what Allah knew of him. He is also said to be the first unbeliever ever. The reason his refusal amounted to disbelief rather than mere sin deserves attention. In the Sharīʿah, failing to carry out an obligation in practice is a sin and a transgression, but it does not make a person an unbeliever. Iblīs became an unbeliever because he defied and challenged a divine command outright, and in refusing to bow he in effect declared that in his judgment Ādam was not worthy of it. He set his own opinion against Allah's decree.

### Why prostration to a creature was once allowed and is now forbidden

Since the Qur'an itself speaks of prostration as a mark of honour, both here and in the story of Yūsuf, it is important to understand what such a prostration was and why Muslims are forbidden it today.

The prostration before Ādam and before Yūsuf cannot have been worship, because worshipping anyone other than Allah is shirk and kufr and could never be permitted by any revealed law. In the time of the earlier prophets, prostrating before someone must therefore have been simply an act of courtesy and respect, with the same value that a greeting, a handshake, the kissing of a hand or standing up in someone's honour has today. Imām al-Jaṣṣāṣ wrote in his Aḥkām al-Qurʾān that the laws of the earlier prophets permitted prostration in honour of one's elders, but that the Sharīʿah of the Prophet ﷺ has forbidden gestures such as prostrating before a person, bowing very low, or standing before someone with the hands folded as in ṣalāh, because all of these may suggest worship, and has allowed only the greeting of salām and the handshake as gestures of courtesy and respect. Ar-Rāzī also held that the prostration was one of greeting and honour.

The reason behind the prohibition is easy to see. Shirk, disbelief and the worship of anything besides Allah contradict the very principle of īmān, so no revealed law could ever tolerate them. But there are acts and gestures which are not themselves shirk or disbelief and yet, through people's ignorance or carelessness, can become a prelude to them. The earlier laws did not forbid such acts absolutely. They only prevented them from being used as instruments of shirk. Making pictures of living things, for instance, is not in itself shirk and was permitted in earlier laws. The Qur'an says of the jinn who served Sulaymān (Solomon) that "they made for him whatever he desired of sanctuaries, statues, basins as large as reservoirs, and cooking pots fixed into the ground" (34:13). In the same way, prostration as a gesture of respect was permitted. But over time the practice opened the way to shirk through people's ignorance and thoughtlessness, and even produced grave distortions in the laws of various prophets, which later prophets and later laws had to correct.

The Prophet ﷺ is the last of the prophets and messengers, and his Sharīʿah is the last of the revealed laws, valid until the end of time. To protect it from every distortion, Allah closed every gap through which shirk or idolatry could possibly enter, and this law therefore strictly forbids all the practices that had at one time or another served as a path to shirk or idol worship. Making pictures of living things has been banned completely. Prostrating before anyone is forbidden, respect being no excuse. It is not permitted to offer ṣalāh at the hours of the day that the idolaters had set apart for worshipping their gods, since even this slight external resemblance might lead toward shirk. And according to a hadith reported by Muslim, a master may not call his slave "my ʿabd" nor may a slave call his master "my rabb," words that merely mean "servant" and "one who nurtures" and are harmless in themselves, but that could be misread and could tempt ignorant slaves or subjugated people into worshipping their masters.

Some reliable scholars add a further explanation concerning prostration in particular. Ṣalāh, the basic form of Islamic worship, consists of four kinds of action: standing, bowing, sitting and prostrating. Standing and sitting are things people do all day in the course of ordinary life, and they are also performed as acts of worship within the prayer. Bowing and prostrating, on the other hand, are not ordinary habitual movements. They are characteristically associated with ṣalāh and with worship, so the Islamic Sharīʿah has identified them as acts of worship and forbidden Muslims to bow or prostrate before anyone but Allah.

On what grounds is it affirmed that the Islamic law has forbidden the practice, given that the Qur'an mentions it with approval in earlier times? Several well-known reports from the Prophet ﷺ, transmitted through a large number of his Companions, establish that prostrating before someone as a mark of respect is unlawful (ḥarām). The best known is the hadith in which Muʿādh told the Prophet ﷺ that he had visited ash-Shām and found the people there prostrating before their priests and scholars, and said that the Messenger of Allah was more deserving of prostration than they. The Prophet ﷺ answered no, and said that if he were to command any human being to prostrate before another, it would be the wife whom he commanded to prostrate to her husband, so great is his right over her. This settles that prostrating out of respect is absolutely forbidden, with no exception for any created being whatsoever. The hadith has come down through twenty Companions, while according to Tadrīb ar-Rāwī, the famous work on the principles of hadith, a report transmitted by as few as ten Companions is already classed as mutawātir and carries the same authority in matters of law as the Qur'an itself.

### How could the Peacock of the Angels fall?

Iblīs had reached such a height of knowledge and learning that he was called Ṭāʾūs al-Malāʾikah, the Peacock of the Angels. How, then, did he come to commit so ruinous an error? Some scholars say that because of his pride and vanity Allah took back from him the wealth of knowledge and understanding he had been given, so that he behaved like an ignorant fool. Others trace his error to self-love and ambition. A line of Arabic verse has been quoted to settle the matter: once Allah's help is withdrawn from a person, he can no longer save himself from sin, and every effort he makes only drives him deeper into misguidance. May Allah in His mercy save us all from such a fate. The lesson drawn is that no one should be vain about his learning, his deeds or even his faith, for faith counts only if it lasts to the final breath and into the first stage of the journey to the next world.

### A reading for the inner life

Majestic and all-compelling is the God of the world and of its people: the Enactor, the Knower of the hidden, eternally beautiful in His doing, tremendous in rank. He is never ignorant of anything He knows, never regrets anything He bestows, is never at a loss over anything He has done. To some He makes attractive what He disapproves, and for others He makes ugly what He approves. Out of fire He created the despairing Iblīs, gave him a place at the Lote Tree of the Furthest Boundary, and sent the angels nearest the Presence to seek knowledge from him. Yet in spite of such distinction and rank, He wrote out for him the inscription of wretchedness and bound his waist with the sash of the curse. Ādam He pulled up out of dark dust, and then the Higher Assembly were made to carry his throne, the cape of exaltedness was laid on his shoulders, set the crown of generosity on his head, and said to the angels of the Presence, "Prostrate before Adam!"

It has come down in the traditions that Ādam was seated on a throne with seven hundred legs, each a journey of seven hundred years from the next, and the command went out to Jibrīl (Gabriel), Mīkāʾīl (Michael) and the chiefs of the angels. The throne was set before the Majestic Throne, and the angels were told to go to it and prostrate before Ādam. When they came and looked at him, they were all intoxicated by his beauty. A face adorned by the God of heaven needs no hairdresser's touch. They saw a beauty without end: the crown of "He created Ādam in His form" upon his head, the robe of "had a spirit of My Own creation breathed into him" (15:29) upon his body, and the embroidery of the loving care of "who love Him and are loved by Him" (5:54) upon the sleeve of his sinlessness. Strangers though we are, with hearts in disarray, we are serving-boys of that world-adorning face.

Describing Ādam, Wahb ibn Munabbih said that God gave him the most beautiful of forms at his creation and dressed him in the Garden's ornaments: rings on all ten fingers, anklets on his legs, bracelets on his arms, a crown and diadem on his head and brow, and gave him as a title the name most beloved to Him, calling him Abū Muḥammad. Then He told him to walk around the Garden and see whether anyone resembled him or whether any creature had been created more beautiful than he. Ādam wandered through the Garden and grew conceited, striding proudly through it. God found that beautiful in him, and from beyond the Throne He called: go on being conceited, Ādam, since the likes of you may be. I loved something, so I made it solitary for the Solitary. That conceit God afterwards passed on to Ādam's offspring. In the ignorant it appears as arrogance, in kings as pridefulness, and in the friends of Allah as ecstasy.

Good fortune in the spirit and in the world is no game, and felicity cannot be bought. Iblīs saw only the suffering of passing days and the toil of the work, while Ādam went to Paradise. Iblīs had obedience without end, yet it was Ādam who received the address of honour. The difference between them was never the quantity of worship. It was the acceptance of Allah's choice.

### In short

- Allah commanded the angels, and with them every being of understanding, to prostrate before Ādam as a visible sign of his superiority. The prostration was a bow of honour and greeting, like that of Yūsuf's family (12:100). The obedience was to Allah.
- Iblīs, a jinn living among the angels and once called ʿAzāzīl, refused out of pride, claiming that fire is better than clay. Arrogance was the first sin, and because he challenged Allah's command outright his refusal was disbelief, not merely disobedience.
- Prostration out of respect was permitted in earlier laws but is forbidden in the final Sharīʿah, which closed every door to shirk. The Prophet ﷺ said that if anyone were to prostrate to a human being it would be a wife to her husband, and he permitted no one.
- Even the Peacock of the Angels fell when Allah's help was withdrawn, so no one should be vain about knowledge, deeds or faith.

35.text:
The story of Ādam (Adam) moves from honour to trial. His superiority had been shown to the angels and acknowledged by them, Iblīs had been condemned for his pride, and now Ādam and his wife received a home. "We cautioned, 'O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.'" The verse contains an unlimited permission and a single prohibition. Everything in the Garden was theirs, with one exception, and that exception became the test. Since Iblīs had been disgraced on Ādam's account, he had a score to settle, and the following verse tells how he used this one forbidden thing to bring about their fall.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We cautioned, 'O Adam!'"** is Allah speaking directly to Ādam. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr ibn Mardawayh reported that Abū Dharr asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ whether Ādam was a prophet, and he answered that he was, a prophet and also a messenger, one whom Allah addressed directly, and this verse is an instance of that address.

**"Live with your wife in Paradise"** shows that Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) had already been created before Ādam entered the Garden, as Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq pointed out. He related that after Allah had finished rebuking Iblīs and had taught Ādam the names of everything, Ādam fell asleep. According to the People of the Book and scholars such as Ibn ʿAbbās, Allah took one of the ribs from his left side and caused flesh to grow in its place while he slept, unaware, and from the rib He created Ḥawwāʾ as a woman, so that she might be a comfort to him. When he woke and saw her beside him he is reported to have said, "My flesh and my blood, my wife," and he found rest in her. When Allah had joined them in marriage and given him this comfort, He addressed him with the words of this verse. Some scholars conclude from the order of events that Ādam was created and the angels prostrated to him somewhere outside Paradise, and that he was brought there afterwards. The words of the Qur'an do not rule out the other possibility, that everything happened inside Paradise and that he was simply told later where he was to live.

The wording also carries legal meaning. In granting permission to eat and in forbidding the tree, Allah used the dual form and addressed both husband and wife. But in assigning the dwelling, He did not address them both. He said to Ādam, "Live, you and your wife." From this difference jurists derive two principles: the husband is responsible for providing his wife with a dwelling, and in the matter of residence the wife follows the husband and lives in the house where he lives. The verb "live" (uskun) itself suggests a temporary stay rather than ownership. Allah did not say that Paradise had been given to them, only that they should dwell there, for He knew that events were coming that would require them to leave it. Besides, the right to own a home in Paradise is earned through faith and good deeds and comes only after the Day of Judgment. The jurists have derived from this that if a man invites someone to live in his house, the guest acquires neither ownership of it nor a right to stay permanently.

**"and eat as freely as you please"** is translated from the Arabic raghadan, which describes provision that one does not have to work for and that never runs out or falls short. Their life was wholly free of care. They were allowed to eat of its food without restriction, from anywhere in the Garden and whenever they wished. Because the verb "eat" is in the dual, the wife is not subordinate to her husband in the matter of food. She may eat whatever she needs or likes, just as he may. And because they were allowed to eat "wherever you will," a person has the right to move freely from place to place according to his needs and wishes.

**"but do not approach this tree"** is an emphatic way of saying "do not eat from it." Allah did not want them to eat its fruit, and as a precaution He forbade them even to go near it. From this the jurists derive a basic principle of Islamic law: whatever is likely to serve as a means or instrument of sin is forbidden along with the sin. Some things are not forbidden in themselves, yet when there is a real danger that using them will draw a person into an unlawful act, they too become forbidden.

What was the tree? Neither the Qur'an nor the hadith names it. Some scholars said it was wheat, others the grapevine, barley, the date palm or the fig tree. Some said it was a tree whose fruit relieves the eater of the need to answer the call of nature, and others that it was the tree from which the angels eat so as to live forever. Another description calls it the tree of knowledge, comprising every type and kind. Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr gave what is held to be the correct position: Allah forbade Ādam and his wife a certain tree in Paradise and they ate from it, but we do not know which tree it was, because neither the Qur'an nor the authentic Sunnah tells us. It may have been barley, a grape or a fig, but knowing this brings no benefit, just as not knowing it brings no harm. Ar-Rāzī took the same position, and al-Qurṭubī likewise saw no need to specify what the Qur'an has left unspecified. Even the Bible does not name the tree. The popular idea that the fruit was an apple arose from nothing more than a pun in Latin, where the word malum means both "apple" and "evil."

**"or else you will be wrongdoers"** means transgressors who have overstepped a limit, and also those who harm themselves, for the loss that followed fell on them.

### How could a prophet disobey?

Ādam had been forbidden the tree and warned against his enemy Satan, and yet he ate from it. On the surface this looks like a sin, while the Qur'an, the hadith and reason all establish that prophets are protected from sin. The four great Imāms of law and all reliable scholars agree that every prophet is protected from all sins, major and minor. A few have suggested that prophets are not protected from minor sins, but the majority reject this. The protection is necessary because prophets are sent as guides. If a guide could break Allah's commands and sin, even in small matters, people could no longer trust his word or his example, and if the prophets themselves cannot be trusted, guidance becomes impossible.

The Qur'an does, however, relate a few incidents that appear to show a prophet committing a fault and drawing Allah's displeasure, and Ādam's eating from the tree is one of them. The agreed explanation is that whenever a prophet errs, it is through a misunderstanding or simple forgetfulness, never through deliberate and wilful defiance of a command. A mujtahid, a scholar qualified to work out by analogy the ruling of a case not explicitly covered by the Qur'an or the hadith, is rewarded by Allah for his effort even when his conclusion is mistaken. A prophet's error is always of this kind, or is due to oversight, and is therefore pardonable and not a sin in the technical sense. Moreover, a prophet is under Allah's protection and can never slip or forget in matters that concern his prophetic and legislative function, but only in personal matters. The rank of the prophets is so exalted, however, that even a small oversight in a great man is treated as a great error. That is why such slips are described in the Qur'an as "sins" and meet with Allah's displeasure, although they are not sins in their nature.

As for Ādam's own error, several explanations have been offered. The first is that a particular tree was pointed out to him as forbidden, but the prohibition was meant to cover every tree of that kind, not that one tree alone. The hadith records a comparable case. The Prophet ﷺ once held up a piece of silk and some gold and said that these two were forbidden to the men of his Ummah, and the ban plainly covers silk and gold as such, not merely the pieces in his hand, though someone might imagine otherwise. Ādam supposed that only the one tree shown to him was forbidden. Satan exploited this misunderstanding, swore to him that as a well-wisher he could never advise anything wrong or harmful, and assured him that the forbidden tree was a different one from the tree he was urging him to pick from. The second explanation is that Satan suggested that the prohibition had applied only for a period after Ādam's creation, as infants are kept from heavy food until they grow, and that now that Ādam was stronger the ban had been lifted. The third is that when Satan told him that eating the fruit would guarantee him eternal bliss in Paradise, Ādam simply forgot the prohibition, and the Qur'an lends weight to this when it says, "And indeed, We once made a covenant with Adam, but he forgot, and so We did not find determination in him" (20:115). Whichever explanation is right, the essential point stands: Ādam did not wilfully disobey Allah. What he did was an oversight, or the kind of mistake a mujtahid can make. It was not properly a sin, but because of his closeness to Allah and his rank as a prophet even this lapse was treated as serious and called a sin, and when he repented and asked pardon, Allah forgave him.

### The two paths

When Allah made Ādam stand before the angels and Iblīs and tested them all with the command to bow, He was giving the first man a practical demonstration of the two paths that would lie open to his descendants. They could follow the example of the angels and bow to God's command even when it meant bowing to someone they considered beneath them, or they could be proud like Satan and refuse. This is the test every human being faces throughout life. On earth a person is constantly presented with the same two alternatives: to bow before truth and justice in all he does, as the angels bowed, or to let arrogance and contempt govern him and deny others their due, as Satan did. The forbidden tree then shows the second half of the lesson: how a person goes astray by letting Satan deceive him into crossing the limits God has set.

### A reading for the inner life

The Sufis have preserved several encounters with Iblīs that turn on this verse. It is said that Iblīs once met Ādam and told him: understand that your face has been made white and mine black, but do not let that delude you. We are like an almond tree planted by a gardener. The tree bears fruit, the fruit goes to the grocer, and some of it is sold to a happy customer and some to a grieving one. The grieving man blackens the almonds and scatters them on the coffin of his dead, while the happy man mixes them with sugar and hands them out white in his joy. I am the black almonds scattered over coffins, and the almonds given out in happiness are the work of your good fortune. But remember that the gardener is one, and we drank from the same stream. Whoever falls among the roses will smell roses, and whoever falls into the gardener's thorns will have his eyes pierced by them.

Dhu'l-Nūn al-Miṣrī said that out in the desert he came upon Iblīs, whose head had not risen from prostration in forty days. He said to him, "Poor wretch, after rejection and the curse, what is all this worship?" Iblīs answered, "O Dhu'l-Nūn, I may have been dismissed from servanthood, but He has not been dismissed from lordship."

Sahl ibn ʿAbdallāh at-Tustarī said that he came across Iblīs one day and said, "I seek refuge in God from you." Iblīs replied, "O Sahl, if you seek refuge in God from me, I seek refuge in God from God. If you say you seek help against the hand of Iblīs, I say I seek help against the hand of the All-Merciful." Sahl asked him why he had not prostrated to Ādam, and Iblīs said, "Leave these foolish words. If I have a road to the Presence, show it to me. Do you want to pin the blame on me? Just now I was at Ādam's grave. I made a thousand prostrations there and rubbed the dust of his grave on my eyes, and in the end I heard the call: 'Do not take the trouble. We do not want you.'" Then he handed Sahl a piece of writing and vanished as Sahl began to read it. On it was written: "Though I erred, destiny did not. Blame me if you wish, Sahl, or leave me be."

Abū Yazīd al-Basṭāmī said that he asked God to show him Iblīs and found him in the sanctuary at Makkah, speaking clever words. He said, "Wretch, with all this cleverness, why did you hold back from the command of the Real?" Iblīs said, "That was a command of trial, not a command of desire. Had it been a command of desire, I would never have held back." Abū Yazīd asked whether it was opposition to the Real that had brought him to this. Iblīs said, "Opposition is one opposite set against another, but God has no opposite. Conformity is one like beside another like, but God has no like. Do you imagine that my conformity with Him comes from me and my opposition from me? Both come from Him, and no one has any power over Him. And despite all that has happened, I hope for mercy, for He has said, 'My mercy encompasses everything' (7:156), and I am a thing." Abū Yazīd objected that the verse goes on to make godfearing a condition. Iblīs said, "Conditions are for someone who does not know how things will turn out. Nothing is hidden from this Lord." Then he disappeared. These stories are not told to excuse Iblīs. They are told to show that worship without submission to Allah's choice is worth nothing, and that no one should rest on his own obedience.

### In short

- Allah settled Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ in Paradise with free and effortless provision and forbade them a single tree, which neither the Qur'an nor the Sunnah identifies and which there is no benefit in identifying.
- The wording yields legal principles: the husband provides the home and the wife lives where he lives, the wife eats as freely as the husband, people may move about freely, and whatever leads to sin is forbidden like the sin.
- Prophets are protected from sin. Ādam's eating was a misunderstanding or forgetfulness (20:115) exploited by Satan's oath, not wilful disobedience, and it is called a sin only because of his exalted rank.
- The prostration and the tree together set out the two paths before every human being: bow to Allah's command like the angels, or refuse like Satan.

36.text:
The test did not last. "But Satan deceived them, leading to their fall from the blissful state they were in, and We said, 'Descend from the heavens to the earth as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.'" Satan kept whispering to them until they ate from the tree they had been forbidden, and the life of effortless ease came to an end. They were sent down to the earth, warned that enmity would spoil life there, and told that their stay on earth would itself be temporary.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But Satan deceived them, leading to their fall"** translates fa-azallahumā, "caused them to slip." The Arabic allows two readings of "from it." It may mean "from Paradise," so that Satan caused them to be removed from it, which is how ʿĀṣim ibn Abī an-Najūd recited the verse, and there is a variant reading, fa-azālahumā, that means exactly that, "he removed them from it." Or it may refer to the tree, in which case the verse means that he tripped them by means of it, as al-Ḥasan and Qatādah explained. The sense then is "because of the tree," just as the Qur'an says elsewhere that a person is "turned away from it" (51:9), meaning turned aside from the truth by some cause. Satan accomplished this by asking them whether he should show them the tree of immortality and a kingdom that never fades, and by swearing to them by God that he was giving them sincere advice, "I am truly your sincere advisor" (7:21), so they ate from it.

The choice of the word "slip" is itself significant. It shows that the error of Ādam (Adam) and Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) was not the kind of disobedience that technically counts as a sin. It arose from a misunderstanding that Satan engineered. They ate because they had been cleverly deceived.

**"from the blissful state they were in"** refers to the clothing, the spacious dwelling and the comfortable provision they had enjoyed. The Qur'an says that Satan "brought them out" of this state, but in fact they left under a divine command. Because Satan served as the means and the intermediary, the action is attributed to him. His role gives him no independent power whatsoever, and any notion of two rival powers in the universe is ruled out completely.

**"and We said, 'Descend from the heavens to the earth as enemies to each other'"** is addressed to Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ and all who would come from them, and on some accounts also to the serpent and the peacock. Who exactly is meant by "enemies to each other" depends on whether Satan was still in the heavens. If he had not yet been expelled from the skies, he is included in the address, and the meaning is that the enmity between Satan on one side and Ādam, Ḥawwāʾ and their descendants on the other would continue on the earth. If, as some scholars hold, he had already been cast out, then the address is to Ādam, Ḥawwāʾ and their progeny, and the implication is a double punishment: banishment from Paradise and the pain of seeing enmity arise among their children through their wronging one another, which no parent can bear easily.

**"You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay"** promises a dwelling place, a livelihood from the earth's produce, and a limited span of life, until death and until the Day of Resurrection. The earth was to be a temporary dwelling that they would also have to leave, which meant that they would never find complete peace of mind there.

### Iblīs and Shayṭān

In the previous episode the Qur'an called him Iblīs, a name from the root balasa, "to be disappointed," meaning one who has lost all hope of Allah's grace. Here he is called ash-Shayṭān, from the root shaṭana, "to be far away," meaning one who has been removed far from Allah's mercy. Iblīs is a personal name. Shayṭān names a kind. When the Qur'an says ash-Shayṭān with the definite article it always means Iblīs, but the common noun shayṭān, and its plural shayāṭīn, covers the whole kind, which includes both human beings and jinn. It is also possible that the word is connected with the root shayṭ, which means an excess of anger and rage.

### How did Satan reach them?

If the Paradise from which Ādam was expelled was in the heavens, as the majority of scholars hold, how could Iblīs enter it after Allah had already expelled him for refusing to prostrate? The majority answer that Satan was indeed barred from Paradise but that there were times when he slipped in secretly. The Tawrāh, for example, says that Iblīs hid inside the mouth of the serpent and entered that way. Some scholars suggest that he misled Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ while he was on his way out of Paradise. Others, including az-Zamakhsharī, say that he was already on the earth and tempted them while they were still in heaven. He may never have met them at all, but planted the suggestion in their minds from a distance, something Satan is always able to do and of which hypnotism offers a faint example. Or, being one of the jinn, who have been given certain powers denied to human beings, he may have taken the form of a serpent or of something else and so got in. Perhaps it was because of this disguise that Ādam did not recall Allah's warning that Satan was his enemy. Since Satan swore to them that he was their well-wisher, it seems that he really did meet them and speak with them face to face. Al-Qurṭubī gathered at this point several useful hadiths about snakes and the ruling on killing them.

### Reports about the descent

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated that Ubayy ibn Kaʿb reported the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying that Allah created Ādam tall, with thick hair, like a date palm heavy with branches. When he ate from the tree his covering fell away and the first thing exposed was his nakedness. Seeing it, he ran through Paradise until his hair caught in a tree, and as he struggled to free himself the Most Merciful called to him, "Ādam, are you running away from Me?" Hearing the words of the Most Merciful, he said, "No, my Lord, but I am ashamed."

Al-Ḥākim recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said that Ādam lived in Paradise only for the stretch of time between the ʿAṣr prayer and sunset, and al-Ḥākim judged this report ṣaḥīḥ by the standard of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, though they did not include it. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Ibn ʿAbbās saying that the place where Allah set Ādam down was called Dahnā and lay between Makkah and aṭ-Ṭāʾif. According to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ādam came down in India and Ḥawwāʾ at Jeddah, that Iblīs came down at Dustumaysān, some miles from Basra, and that the serpent came down at Aṣbahān. Muslim and an-Nasāʾī recorded that Abū Hurayrah reported the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying that of all the days on which the sun rises, Friday is the best: Ādam was created on it, admitted to Paradise on it, and sent out of it on it.

### A reading for the inner life

Consider the wonder of it. First Allah caressed His servant and put his small affairs in order. Then He threw him into turmoil, undid what He had arranged for him, and rebuked him on top of it. The Pīr of the Ṭarīqah prayed: O God, You show Your friends to their enemies and hand the poor over to heartache and grief. You make them ill and then nurse them Yourself. You make them helpless and then heal them Yourself. You made Ādam from dust and then dealt so beautifully with him. You wrote his happiness at the top of the ledger and made him Your guest in Paradise. You seated him in the garden of approval and made a pact with him not to eat the wheat, while hiding in Your unseen knowledge that he would eat it. Then You put him in prison and made him weep for years. Your all-compelling power does what compellers do and Your lordship does what lords do, and all Your rebukes and all Your war are aimed at Your friends.

The Pīr was asked whether Ādam was more complete in this world or in Paradise. He answered that he was more complete in this world, because in Paradise he came under suspicion through his own self, while in this world he came under suspicion through passion. And he warned against thinking that Ādam was taken out of Paradise because of any lowliness in him. The real cause was how grand his aspiration was. Passion's petitioner came knocking at the door of Ādam's breast and said: the beauty of meaning has been unveiled, and you are still sitting in the abode of ease. Ādam saw an infinite beauty beside which the beauty of the eight paradises was nothing, and his high aspiration tightened its belt and said: if you are ever going to fall in love, it must be with that. Then came the command: Ādam, you have stepped into passion's street now, so leave Paradise, which is the house of ease.

### In short

- Satan made them slip, either out of Paradise or by means of the tree, through a whisper about immortality and a false oath of goodwill (7:21). The word "slip" shows that their fault was a deception-induced error, not a wilful sin.
- They were sent down with the warning of mutual enmity, whether between Satan and humanity or among human beings themselves, and told that the earth would be a temporary home with provision until death.
- Scholars differ on how Satan reached them in a Paradise he had been expelled from, whether by stealth, through the serpent, from a distance or on his way out.
- Reports describe Ādam's height, the brevity of his stay, the places where each of them came down, and Friday as the day of his creation, admission and departure.

37.text:
The fall was not the end. "Then Adam was inspired with words of prayer by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful." The loss of Paradise was real but not irretrievable. Ādam (Adam) still had the chance to turn back to his Lord, put right what he had done and ask forgiveness, and when he did, Allah relented toward him and cleansed him of his fault as though it had never been. This verse establishes, at the very beginning of human history, that repentance is the way back.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then Adam was inspired with words of prayer by his Lord"** means that Ādam learned from his Lord, or was taught and inspired with, certain words, which became a path to repentance for him and for his descendants after him. The Arabic allows a second reading in which "the words" is the subject and "Ādam" the object, so that the words came to Ādam, and the meaning is the same. A long line of early scholars identify the words with the prayer recorded in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf. Among them are Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Khālid ibn Maʿdān, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam. The prayer is: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers" (7:23). With these words he prayed.

As-Suddī reported another account from Ibn ʿAbbās. Ādam said, "My Lord, did You not create me with Your own Hands?" He was told yes. "And breathe into me of Your spirit?" Yes. "And when I sneezed, You said, 'May Allah have mercy on you.' Does Your mercy not precede Your anger?" Yes. "And did You decree that I would do this deed?" Yes. "Then if I repent, will You return me to Paradise?" And Allah said yes. Similar reports come from al-ʿAwfī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Saʿīd ibn Maʿbad on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥākim recorded this report in his Mustadrak from Ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās, stating that its chain is ṣaḥīḥ although al-Bukhārī and Muslim did not record it.

**"so He accepted his repentance"** means that He relented toward him and forgave him. Satan had sworn to them that he was their sincere adviser (7:21), and they had been deceived, but the moment they regretted it and turned back, the door was open.

**"Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful"** gives the reason. Allah forgives whoever regrets his error and returns to Him. He overlooks misdeeds and shows mercy to everyone who dies repentant. The same promise runs through the Qur'an: "Do they not know that Allah alone accepts the repentance of His servants and receives their charity, and that Allah alone is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful" (9:104), and, "Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah's forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110), and, "And whoever repents and does good has truly turned to Allah properly" (25:71). These verses testify that Allah forgives the sins of all who repent, out of His kindness and mercy toward His creatures. There is no god but Allah, the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful.

### A reading for the inner life

Notice that Allah speaks here with the lid on. He says that Ādam received words, but He does not disclose what passed between them, so that the secrets of love would not spill into the open and love's story would stay concealed. A poet once said to his beloved, "Halt," and she answered only, "Qāf," the first letter of the word. She did not say "I have halted," which would have given the secret away to the watchers, nor "I will not halt," which would have wounded the lover's heart. Though the ordinary language of commentary does not say so, the people of allusion suggest that the words were like what lovers say at parting: when you leave me, do not forget my covenant, and even if your awareness of me should fade one day, do not prefer another to me.
